KEY MESSAGE 1...Latest obs show a weak area of low pressure
currently about 300 miles east of Cape Hatteras with showers
wrapping around this low, mainly across the offshore waters. In
addition to this, latest obs show widespread NE'rly winds 
gusting to 35-45 mph along the OBX and coast with winds 
decreasing the further inland you go to about 10-20 mph. 

Overall not much change in forecast thinking as a mid level
shortwave is forecast to round the base of an upper level trough
currently located along the Eastern Seaboard today into tonight.
This mid level shortwave will act to rapidly deepen the 
aforementioned surface low as it slowly shifts north in the 
coming days, bringing a prolonged period of gusty N/NE winds and
dangerous coastal and marine conditions to ENC. Uncertainty 
still exists with the eventual strength and exact track of the 
low as it shifts off towards the New England coast as we 
approach this weekend. Latest guidance is still rather split
with the Canadian and GFS deterministic and ensemble guidance
further east than the ICON, ECMWF and its ensembles. This is 
mainly owed to the fact the the ECMWF and ICON have the low
starting to deepen slightly earlier and these solutions have a 
more consolidated low today while the GFS and Canadian guidance 
suggests a complex low will remain in place today into tomorrow 
with the northern lobe becoming the dominant low over the next 
few days as it deepens. We look to get some further clarity 
today into tonight as we will see exactly where this low will 
set up as it deepens which will go a long way in determining 
exact duration of impacts for ENC. This results in continued low
to moderate confidence on the end time of hazardous marine 
conditions and coastal impacts.

Regarding sensible weather, scattered showers and isolated 
thunderstorms along the coast are expected to persist through 
today. Flooding risk remains very low.

By far, the greatest impacts with this coastal low remain across 
the Outer Banks. Here, continued moderate to strong northeast 
to north winds remain in place, and potentially last into 
Saturday morning, especially if the ECMWF/ICON solutions are
correct. Probabilistic guidance continues to show a strong 
signal for reaching Wind Advisory criteria with both sustained 
winds and gusts, and the wind advisory for Dare County, 
Ocracoke, and Downeast Carteret County remains in effect. For 
the OBX from Cape Hatteras north, peak gusts could top out 
around 50 mph, and this may lead to some minor tree and power 
line damage, along with a risk of isolated power outages. Roads 
along the Outer Banks may be dangerous to traverse for high 
profile vehicles, especially along bridges.

The strong, and long duration, of the winds is also expected to
support an increased risk of coastal impacts. Seas are already
dangerous, reaching heights of about 13-16 ft at 13-14 seconds 
north of Cape Hatteras and already up to around 10 ft across the
outer waters of Onslow Bay as of this update. Seas likely peak 
around 15-20 ft today into tonight creating dangerous surf 
conditions in addition to a risk of beach erosion, wave runup, 
ocean overwash, and minor to moderate coastal flooding. Of 
note, the highest wave energy appears to be aligned with the 
evening high tide today (which happens to be the highest of the
two high tides today). This will likely result in impacts to 
vulnerable portions of the Outer Banks north of Ocracoke Inlet 
where dune structures are compromised or non-existent. At this 
point the 6-8ft+ wave heights in the surf zone may last into 
this weekend. A High Surf Advisory Remains in effect through 
Saturday evening.

For soundside areas adjacent to the southern Pamlico Sound, and
the nearby Neuse River, persistent north to northeasterly winds
may lead to minor coastal flooding through Friday. Already, 
some gauges in the southern Pamlico Sound are approaching or 
have reached minor flood levels. Eventually the winds are 
expected to turn more northerly, which may then allow the 
soundside coastal flooding risk to shift to portions of Ocracoke
and Hatteras Villages.

Please continue to stay tuned for future updates as this is a
complex and longer-duration coastal low event, with subtle
changes in strength and path of the low leading to increased, or
decreased, coastal impacts.

KEY MESSAGE 2...
As the low shifts to New England and eventually weakens, sfc 
high and ridging aloft builds into ENC early next week. This 
will bring lighter winds, sunshine, and warmer weather back to 
the region. Of note, despite the warming weather, light 
northerly to variable winds early next week are forecast to keep
dewpoints in the 50s, making for more comfortable conditions 
despite highs warming up into the mid to upper 80s.
